frames.title: SubInvoker.ApplySingle / Explain
frames.explanation: A third root node, kept deliberately short: what it is here for is a STAIRCASE of row lengths, so four same-editor links off four different pairs of rows each route to a different column.

relations.note: the shortest reach of the five - two 49-column rows, so this lane routes furthest left
a little wider - 59 columns, so this lane sits one column out from the first
wider again - 78 columns of dictionary, and the third column out
the widest same-editor reach - 96 columns, and the last column before the portals
the portal, outside every one of them whatever its own row is worth

steps.explanation: Five token links off one line, all diving
steps.note: FIVE links leave line 18, and every one of them has a target below it. Rail 0 runs in the row's own top leading; rails 1-4 are 3px higher each, and line 18 has bought itself the 13px of blank space they need rather than borrowing it from the row above. Each link also gets its own lane: all five are same-editor links, so the lanes are 12px apart and the whole fan is 52px wide. Links 3 and 4 land on the SAME row (23) — so the fan happens at both ends, where the far rows need one rail each and buy nothing.
steps.ttsText: Five links leave the method signature at once. Each one is numbered, and the number decides how far its rail sits above the row and how far its channel sits to the right — so five links off one line are five separate lines rather than one thick one.

steps.explanation: Five token links off one line, all rising
steps.note: The mirror of the step before it: five links leave line 31 and every target is above it, so every rail runs along the row's BOTTOM leading and the space is bought below rather than above. Links 2 and 3 both land on row 26. The colours are the same five lanes in the same order, which is what makes 'the blue one' mean the same thing on both steps.
steps.ttsText: Now the same five-link fan the other way up. The targets are all above, so every rail leaves the bottom of the row and the fan spreads downward. The colours are the same, in the same order.

steps.explanation: Five line links off one line
steps.note: The other anchor, and the one round 7 rerouted. None of these ten endpoints names a token, so every end hangs off the END of its row's text — and every one of them is a same-editor link, so every one runs along the CENTRE of its row for the whole span, turns once down its own lane, and turns once back into its target's row. No rail, no U-turn: 'just turn to target'. Line 54 is a closing brace, so its five ends start well left of the code and the runs are long.
steps.ttsText: The second kind of link hangs off the end of a row rather than off a token. It turns up or down onto the same rail every link uses, and from there on the drawing is identical.

steps.explanation: Three same-editor links and two portals — line level
steps.note: The mix, and the reason lanes are ordered rather than merely numbered. Five links leave line 68; three of them stay in this editor and two leave it. The three same-editor links take the INNER lanes, 12px apart, because a same-editor vertical is one stroke wide; the two portals take the outer lanes, a whole portal apart, because a portal is 23px wide and nothing may be routed through one. No endpoint names a token, so every end leaves the END of its row's text and runs along the row's own middle — and only the two portal links climb onto a rail at all, in the last 26px before their portal.
steps.ttsText: Now a step with both joins at once. Three links stay in this editor and two leave it. The three that stay take the inner lanes, because a line needs a stroke of width; the two that leave take the outer ones, because a portal needs its own.

steps.explanation: Three same-editor links and two portals — token level
steps.note: The same five lanes with the other anchor. Every end names a token, so every end is tinted and leaves the tint's own corner already on its rail — and hovering any of them brightens the token as well as the link, at BOTH ends, which is what makes a link read as one object rather than as two marks. The two portals land in the AuditHandler node above, whose rows carry the far tint.
steps.ttsText: The same three-and-two mix, anchored on tokens instead of on line ends. Hovering any link brightens its token at both ends, so the whole thing lights up as one object.

steps.explanation: Five links off five DIFFERENT pairs of rows - the routing staircase
steps.note: The step that judges round 8 item 6. Every other step in this plan hangs its links off ONE row, so every lane wants the same clearance and they can only be stacked. Here the four same-editor links reach across four different pairs of rows - 49, 59, 78 and 96 columns wide - and each lane routes to its OWN column, as near its own code as the lanes inside it allow. Round 7 put all four at the widest of them, which is why every label was ellipsized. The portal is still outside all four, because that is a routing rule and not an optimisation. Hover the innermost link: its label has room now.
steps.ttsText: Four links reaching across four different pairs of rows. Each one turns up its own column, as near its own code as it can get, instead of every link being pushed out to the widest row on the step.
